variables.name: Vegetation greenness (NDVI)
variables.question: Greener or browner?
variables.definition: NDVI compares red and near-infrared light reflected by plants; higher values mean denser, healthier green vegetation (−0.2 water/bare … 0.9 dense forest).
variables.provider: NASA LP DAAC; COG mirror on Microsoft Planetary Computer
variables.resolution: 500 m product, quality-screened and averaged to 0.1° grid (≈ 8–11 km)
variables.citation: Didan, K. (2021). MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 Global 500m SIN Grid V061. NASA EOSDIS LP DAAC. doi:10.5067/MODIS/MOD13A1.061
variables.license: NASA EOSDIS data: no restrictions on reuse (NASA Earth Science Data Policy)
caveats: Monthly value = mean of 16-day composites starting in that month, read at the native 500 m resolution and averaged to 0.1°.
Quality-screened: pixels the MODIS quality layer marks as cloudy, snow/ice or missing are removed first; a cell needs at least 20% good pixels in a composite.
Terra's orbit drifted after 2022; the default period stops at 2024.
A change in NDVI can come from land-use change (clearing, irrigation), not only from climate.

variables.name: Daytime land surface temperature
variables.question: Hotter ground by day?

variables.resolution: 1 km product, quality-screened and averaged to 0.1° grid (≈ 8–11 km)
variables.citation: Wan, Z., Hook, S., Hulley, G. (2021). MODIS/Terra Land Surface Temperature/Emissivity 8-Day L3 Global 1km SIN Grid V061. NASA EOSDIS LP DAAC. doi:10.5067/MODIS/MOD11A2.061
variables.license: NASA EOSDIS data: no restrictions on reuse (NASA Earth Science Data Policy)
caveats: Only clear-sky observations exist: cloudy months contribute fewer values (see coverage).
Monthly value = mean of 8-day composites at the native 1 km resolution; pixels the quality layer marks as not produced or with LST error above 2 K are removed first.
Terra's overpass time drifted after 2022; the default period stops at 2024.

variables.name: Afternoon land surface temperature (Aqua)
variables.question: Does a second satellite agree?
variables.definition: Same measurement as the Terra daytime surface temperature, but from the Aqua satellite passing around 13:30 local time; its orbit was kept stable until 2022, so it is a useful cross-check.
variables.provider: NASA LP DAAC; COG mirror on Microsoft Planetary Computer
variables.resolution: 1 km product, quality-screened and averaged to 0.1° grid (≈ 8–11 km)
variables.citation: Wan, Z., Hook, S., Hulley, G. (2021). MODIS/Aqua Land Surface Temperature/Emissivity 8-Day L3 Global 1km SIN Grid V061. NASA EOSDIS LP DAAC. doi:10.5067/MODIS/MYD11A2.061
variables.license: NASA EOSDIS data: no restrictions on reuse (NASA Earth Science Data Policy)
caveats: Aqua starts in mid-2002; the cube starts in 2003 (first complete year).

variables.name: Air temperature at 2 m
variables.question: Warmer air?
variables.definition: Monthly mean air temperature two metres above the ground, from the NASA MERRA-2 reanalysis (a model that assimilates observations).
variables.provider: NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project
variables.citation: NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) POWER Project, funded through the NASA Earth Science/Applied Science Program; MERRA-2 (Gelaro et al., 2017, J. Climate).
variables.license: NASA POWER data: free to use, acknowledgement requested
caveats: Reanalysis = model constrained by observations; not a direct satellite measurement.

variables.name: Precipitation
variables.question: More or less rain?
variables.definition: Average amount of rain and snow reaching the ground per day, from MERRA-2 corrected with observed precipitation.
variables.provider: NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project
variables.citation: NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) POWER Project; MERRA-2 bias-corrected precipitation (Reichle et al., 2017).
variables.license: NASA POWER data: free to use, acknowledgement requested
caveats: Precipitation varies a lot year to year: long periods are needed before a trend is detectable.

variables.name: Precipitation (GPCP, satellites and gauges)
variables.question: Does an independent rain record agree?
variables.definition: Monthly rain and snow from the Global Precipitation Climatology Project, which merges microwave and infrared satellite estimates with rain-gauge analyses (GPCC). It does not come from the MERRA-2 model.
variables.provider: NASA GSFC and University of Maryland (GPCP); distributed by NOAA PSL / NCEI
variables.citation: Adler, R.F. et al. (2018). The Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) Monthly Analysis (New Version 2.3) and a Review of 2017 Global Precipitation. Atmosphere 9, 138. doi:10.3390/atmos9040138. Data: doi:10.7289/V56971M6
variables.license: NOAA NCEI Climate Data Record: no usage restrictions
caveats: Coarse 2.5° grid: a small area uses only a few cells, or the nearest one.

variables.name: Root-zone soil wetness
variables.question: Drier or wetter soil?
variables.definition: How full the soil water store is in the root zone (top ~1 m): 0 = completely dry, 1 = saturated. Modelled by MERRA-2.
variables.provider: NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project
variables.citation: NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) POWER Project; MERRA-2 land surface (Reichle et al., 2017).
variables.license: NASA POWER data: free to use, acknowledgement requested
caveats: Model estimate: irrigation and groundwater pumping are not represented.
Planned independent check: SMAP (2015–) or GRACE water storage (needs Earthdata Login).

methods.deseasonalisation: Each calendar month's mean over the selected period is subtracted (anomalies).
methods.trend: Ordinary least squares slope of the anomalies, reported per decade.
methods.uncertainty: Two memory corrections: month to month (AR(1) for the actual sampling, bias-corrected; Santer et al. 2000) and year to year (the same test on yearly means). The p-value is the larger of the two and the 95% interval covers both, so a trend counts only if both agree.
methods.cross_check: Seasonal Mann–Kendall with the Hirsch & Slack (1984) correction for dependent months, and Mann–Kendall on yearly means with the Hamed & Rao (1998) correction; the larger p is shown. Seasonal Sen slope.
methods.calibration: Checked on synthetic series without a trend: with month-to-month memory up to 0.9, seasons and gaps, at most about 6% are called significant (the target is 5%). Slow decade-long swings remain hard: 5–12% instead of 12–39% before this correction.
methods.map_multiple_testing: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate across map cells, q = 0.05 (Wilks 2016).
methods.period_choice: The map correction covers grid cells, not the choice of period, season or variable: the more combinations you try, the more likely one looks significant by chance. The squares in “Does it hold?” overlap, so they are not independent repeats.
methods.regional_mean: cos(latitude)-weighted mean of cell anomalies; months with < 50% area coverage are dropped.
methods.minimum_data: A trend is computed only if at least 70% of the selected months are valid.

verdict.title: Trend detected
verdict.text: Significant at 5% after correcting for memory in the data. A rank-based test (Mann–Kendall) gives the same result.

answer.question: Warmer air?
answer.headline: Yes – warmer.
lines: The air in Central Europe got warmer: +0.51 °C per decade (1981–2025).
Over 45 years that adds up to about +2.3 °C, 2.3× the usual year-to-year swing (±1 °C).
Across the map, 100% of grid cells went up and 0% went down; 100% show a significant trend after correcting for many tests.
How sure: 133 of 136 other start/end periods give the same direction, 45 of them also significant; a rank-based test (Mann–Kendall) gives the same result.

Independent check with NASA GISTEMP (weather stations), same area, 1981–2025: +0.509 °C per decade; this dataset gives +0.51 for the same years. Both show a significant trend in the same direction; the difference in size is not significant.
answer.caveat: Reanalysis = model constrained by observations; not a direct satellite measurement.

p < 0.001, the stricter of two memory corrections: month to month (effective n ≈ 328 of 540 months) and year to year (45 yearly means).
Mann–Kendall p < 0.001, also corrected for memory; Sen slope +0.49.
Monthly values minus the usual value for each calendar month; 100% valid data.

methods.deseasonalisation: Each calendar month's mean over the selected period is subtracted (anomalies).
methods.trend: Ordinary least squares slope of the anomalies, reported per decade.
methods.uncertainty: Two memory corrections: month to month (AR(1) for the actual sampling, bias-corrected; Santer et al. 2000) and year to year (the same test on yearly means). The p-value is the larger of the two and the 95% interval covers both, so a trend counts only if both agree.
methods.cross_check: Seasonal Mann–Kendall with the Hirsch & Slack (1984) correction for dependent months, and Mann–Kendall on yearly means with the Hamed & Rao (1998) correction; the larger p is shown. Seasonal Sen slope.
methods.calibration: Checked on synthetic series without a trend: with month-to-month memory up to 0.9, seasons and gaps, at most about 6% are called significant (the target is 5%). Slow decade-long swings remain hard: 5–12% instead of 12–39% before this correction.
methods.map_multiple_testing: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate across map cells, q = 0.05 (Wilks 2016).
methods.period_choice: The map correction covers grid cells, not the choice of period, season or variable: the more combinations you try, the more likely one looks significant by chance. The squares in “Does it hold?” overlap, so they are not independent repeats.
methods.regional_mean: cos(latitude)-weighted mean of cell anomalies; months with < 50% area coverage are dropped.
methods.minimum_data: A trend is computed only if at least 70% of the selected months are valid.

limitations.exposure: Regional exposure is one input to a facility risk assessment, which also needs local information about the site and its safeguards.
limitations.history: Historical monthly records show past changes. Weather alerts and climate projections require other data and methods.
limitations.water: Rainfall and soil wetness describe drying conditions. Estimating water supply requires local measurements or a hydrological model.
limitations.heat: Air and land surface temperatures measure different things. Monthly means cannot give hot-day counts or human heat stress.
limitations.shared: The POWER variables share the MERRA-2 reanalysis, so agreement between them does not count as independent confirmation.
limitations.scale: The grid resolution sets the spatial scale. A regional trend cannot describe a building's microclimate.
limitations.causes: Statistical significance describes the evidence for a trend. Its causes require a separate analysis.
limitations.windows: The time windows overlap and share observations.
